title: Mallika the queen
hookLine: Queen Mallika, wise and generous, whose question about beauty and wealth the Buddha answers (AN 4.197)

lines: PLAIN OR BEAUTIFUL, POOR OR RICH.
WHAT SHE DOES WITH THE ANSWER.
cards: Queen Mallika, wife of King Pasenadi of Kosala, comes to the Buddha with a question that sounds almost impolite. Why are some women plain to look at, poor, and without influence?
Why are others plain, but rich and influential? Why are some beautiful but poor and powerless, and others beautiful, rich and influential too? She isn't asking about strangers.
By her own account, she oversees a royal household full of young women from every kind of family, and she fits one of her own four kinds. Today: the answer she gets, and what she does with it.

teach.b: First, the answer, from the Numbered Discourses, the book of fours. The Buddha ties each thing to a habit. A woman who is easily angered and irritable, he says, comes to be plain when she is born again.
One who doesn't give food, drink, clothing, lodging, lamps and the like to ascetics and brahmins comes to be poor. One who envies others' gains and honors comes to have little influence.
Patience, giving and freedom from envy lead the other way. That's karma as this sutta teaches it, across lives: what is done in one life shapes the next.
Some readers also hear in it how habits shape a person here and now. Second, her response. She doesn't argue, and she doesn't make it about anyone else.
She looks at herself: she must have been irritable before, since she is plain now; but she must have given, since she is rich, and been free of envy, since she has influence. Third, her resolve.
From today, she says, I won't be angry.
I will give. I won't be envious. And she goes for refuge.
Fourth, another conversation, in the Connected Discourses. King Pasenadi asks her: is anyone dearer to you than yourself? No one, she answers honestly, and asks him the same; he admits, no one.

When the king tells the Buddha, he answers with a verse: search every direction and you'll find no one dearer than yourself; and since others hold themselves just as dear, one who loves oneself shouldn't harm another.
A queen who could hear a hard truth and turn it into giving.

how: Buddhist teachers draw on the Mallika Sutta when teaching on generosity and karma, and on Mallika and Pasenadi's conversation when teaching that loving oneself is the ground for not harming others.

o: a nun who wore only rough robes
a merchant's wife who fed the monks
a queen who resolved to give freely

games.q: Mallika the queen: tap the pairs.

s: Mallika argued with the Buddha's answer
she looked at herself and resolved not to be angry, to give, and not to envy.
Mallika and Pasenadi both said no one was dearer than themselves
and the Buddha drew from it: so don't harm another.
in the sutta, beauty comes from being rich
the sutta ties being plain to anger, poverty to not giving, and little influence to envy.

games.q: you're a queen. the Buddha says anger, stinginess and envy shape a person's life. what do you do?
o: resolve not to be angry, to give, and not to envy.
ask him about the king instead.
games.why: Mallika looks at herself, resolves to be free of anger and envy and to give, and goes for refuge.

practice: Think of something you give regularly: time, money, a meal, a ride, attention. Notice how you usually give it, gladly, grudgingly, or on autopilot, with no need to judge.
Then picture giving it once the way Mallika resolved to give: freely, with no envy and no irritation in it.

wordCard.voice: Mallika. The queen whose question about beauty and wealth the Buddha answered, and who resolved to give. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Mallika, the queen's name; the same word names the jasmine flower.

carryVoice: Your line: the generous queen. A hard answer became her fresh start. That's day seven hundred sixty-five.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 3.8 (Mallika: no one dearer than oneself)
